title: What a Geotechnical Investigation Is, and How to Read a Borehole Log
summary: Soil is grains, water and air, and its behaviour depends on whether friction or cohesion carries the load. An investigation must be scoped to the foundation actually proposed, and the owner can read a borehole log well enough to spot the findings that matter.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the geotechnical report is the most important document you buy before design, and its value is set by its scope, not its thickness. The depth of the investigation must match the foundation actually proposed, or the report describes ground your building never touches.

In plain English

Soil is made of solid grains with water and air in the spaces between them. In coarse soils such as sand and gravel, strength comes mostly from friction between grains. In fine soils such as clay and silt, it comes mostly from cohesion, the way the particles and water hold together. That difference explains how they fail. A sand failure tends to be sudden. A clay failure is often a building that settles and tilts slowly for years, because water has to squeeze out of the clay before it compresses.

The classification

In American practice soils are described with the Unified Soil Classification System, a two-letter symbol. The first letter names the main type, for example G for gravel, S for sand, M for silt, C for clay, O for organic. The second describes grading or plasticity, for example W for well graded or H for high plasticity. So CH is a high-plasticity clay. The plasticity index, the range of water content over which a clay behaves plastically, predicts how much the soil will swell, shrink and move, more than how strong it is. Organic soil or peat under the footprint is a serious finding, never a footnote, because it compresses a great deal and keeps compressing for years.

How the ground is tested

The Standard Penetration Test drives a sampler into the bottom of a borehole and counts the blows needed to advance it a set distance, giving a sample and a strength index at intervals, often every metre and a half. The Cone Penetration Test pushes an instrumented cone continuously and records resistance all the way down, so it finds thin soft layers that an SPT may step over between samples. Good practice on variable ground uses both: boreholes for samples you can see and test, cones for a continuous profile. Laboratory tests on samples then give moisture content, plasticity, strength and compressibility.

Depth is set by the foundation

A foundation spreads its load into the ground, and the zone that is significantly stressed reaches deeper the wider the loaded area. A commonly quoted rule of thumb is that the stressed zone under a pad extends to roughly twice its width, and under a raft to a depth comparable to its width or more [unverified — confirm independently]. So a report scoped for small pads may be worthless for a raft or for piles.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical report was drilled to 6 metres with three boreholes, for a building originally planned on 3-metre pads.

  1. For 3-metre pads, a stressed zone of about twice the width is about 6 metres: the scope fits.
  2. The design changes to a raft 20 metres wide. Its stressed zone may extend 20 metres or more. The report says nothing about the ground between 6 and 20 metres.
  3. The log at 5.5 metres shows soft grey clay with organic traces, then stops. The single most important layer for the raft is the one nobody sampled.
  4. Groundwater was dipped once, on the day of drilling, at 1.2 metres. On a high water table that number may be wrong by a metre either way across seasons; it is close to worthless for dewatering design.
  5. The fix is a supplementary investigation: deeper boreholes and cones across the footprint and standpipes or piezometers monitored over a stated period. The cost is usually small relative to one wrong foundation decision.

Reading the log

Open the logs yourself and look for five things: how many holes and where, how deep, sample recovery (a poorly recovered sample may hide a soft layer), any organic strata under the footprint, and how groundwater was measured. Then read the recommendations and mark every hedge: "may be suitable", "subject to further investigation", "the contractor should satisfy himself". Hedging reads as caution and functions as risk transfer back to you. Ask what it would take to make each recommendation firm.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating an inherited report, one that came with the land or was drilled for a different building, as a design document. It is background only. The second risk is incentive: under Design-Build, the party who benefits from a thin, cheap investigation may be the party scoping it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner asks whether the report says the ground is adequate. Turn it around: ask what the report would have to omit for bad ground to look acceptable. Shallow holes, few holes, one-day water readings and missing organics are exactly those omissions.

How you will use it

Get the investigation scope in writing before drilling, and have your own geotechnical engineer confirm hole count and depth against the foundation actually proposed. Require SPT sampling plus CPT where ground varies, and groundwater monitored over time through installed instruments. Require the report addressed to you or carrying reliance assignable to you and your lender, with counsel confirming the wording. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer licensed in the jurisdiction.
checklist: Agree the investigation scope in writing before drilling, against the foundation actually proposed.
Require SPT sampling plus CPT profiling where ground is variable.
Require groundwater monitored over a stated period through installed instruments.
Read the logs yourself: hole count, depth, recovery, organics and plasticity of the bearing layer.
Mark every hedged recommendation and ask what would make it firm.
Never treat an inherited report as a design document.
Have the report addressed to you, or with reliance assignable to you and your lender.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: The land came with a geotechnical report: two boreholes to 5 metres, groundwater dipped once, no organics recorded. Your engineer now proposes a raft. Can you rely on the report?
selftest.a: No. It is background only. Two shallow holes cannot describe the ground a wide raft stresses, a single water reading cannot support dewatering or uplift design, and the absence of recorded organics in two holes proves little. Commission a supplementary investigation scoped to the raft, with deeper boreholes, cone profiles and monitored groundwater.

apply: Find any published borehole log and identify the soil symbols, the deepest sample, how groundwater was recorded, and one hedge in the recommendations.
sources: Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM D2487) and SPT (ASTM D1586) and CPT (ASTM D5778) as commonly cited; confirm current editions. Depth of investigation rules of thumb vary by guide and must be set by the geotechnical engineer [unverified — confirm independently]. Example hypothetical.

title: How Ground Works Fail, and the Nicoll Highway Lesson
summary: Ground works fail by face collapse, failure of support systems, groundwater acting from below, and damage to neighbours. The Nicoll Highway collapse shows the pattern that matters most to an owner: warnings that were measured, then explained away.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an excavation is a temporary structure holding back tonnes of soil and water, and it fails in a small number of recognisable ways. The most important pattern is organisational: instruments that read beyond their limits while people revised the limits instead of stopping.

In plain English

When you dig a hole, the soil around it wants to fall in and the water around it wants to flow in or push up from below. Either the soil is sloped back so it stands by itself, or a designed support system holds it, and the water is either kept out or pumped away. When one of those fails, people below can be killed and buildings next door can move.

The four failure families

First, unsupported faces collapse. Soil is heavy, around 1.8 to 2 tonnes per cubic metre, so a shallow collapse can bury and crush a worker; depth is not a reliable measure of danger. Second, engineered support systems fail structurally: a strut buckles, a waling bends, a connection shears, or a prop is removed out of sequence. Third, groundwater acts from below: water pressure under the base lifts it, or seepage carries soil into the hole, which is called piping, or loosens sand until it behaves like a liquid. Fourth, excavation or dewatering damages neighbours: lowering the water table can consolidate clay under an adjacent building and cause it to settle.

The Nicoll Highway collapse

In Singapore in April 2004, a deep excavation for a metro line collapsed beside the Nicoll Highway, killing four people and bringing down part of the road. As the public inquiry described it, instruments measuring wall deflection had read beyond their trigger levels for a long period before the collapse, and the organisational response was to revise the trigger levels rather than stop work and investigate. The inquiry also identified design errors in the support system [unverified — confirm independently]. Read the Committee of Inquiry report before quoting details. The lesson for an owner is not the engineering; it is the decision to explain away a warning.

Monitoring and triggers

A monitoring regime has instruments (inclinometers for wall movement, piezometers for water pressure, settlement points on neighbours), trigger levels, a defined action at each level, and a named responsible person. A typical scheme has a lower level that requires review and increased monitoring, and a higher level that requires stopping and implementing contingency measures. The rule that makes it work is that trigger levels cannot be changed without the design engineer's written agreement and written notice to the owner.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical shored excavation 8 metres deep, with wall deflection triggers of 25 millimetres for review and 40 millimetres for stop.

  1. Week 1, the inclinometer reads 12 millimetres. Below review level; report and continue.
  2. Week 3, it reads 27 millimetres, over the review level. The required action is an engineering review and more frequent readings; it is reported to you as an exception.
  3. Week 4, it reads 34 millimetres, and the contractor proposes raising the triggers to 40 and 60 because "the wall is performing within its capacity". This is the Nicoll Highway moment.
  4. The correct sequence is investigate, then revise: the design engineer explains why movement is larger than predicted, checks the design with the measured data, and only then, in writing, agrees any change. Never revise, then continue.
  5. Meanwhile a settlement point on the neighbouring building shows 8 millimetres. Your dilapidation survey from before the dig shows existing cracks in its wall, so you can tell new movement from old.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is normalising a warning: a reading over trigger that is accepted once becomes the new normal, and the next reading is compared against it. The second risk is silence: if monitoring data stops appearing in reports, the absence is itself the signal.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats cloudy water flowing through a retaining wall as an observation. It is a stop-work condition, because cloudy water carries soil, and soil leaving the ground means voids are forming where nobody can see them. The other mistake is allowing a strut, prop or temporary support to be removed without the design engineer's written approval.

How you will use it

Require temporary works for the excavation to be designed by a qualified engineer and independently checked. Require a monitoring regime with triggers, actions and a named responsible person, and a clause that triggers cannot change without written engineer agreement and notice to you. Make monitoring a standing item at every progress meeting, reported whether or not there is an exception. Require dewatering contingency (standby pumps, alarms, power that survives a weekend). Commission a dilapidation survey of neighbours before breaking ground. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer and temporary works designer; independent checking engineer.
checklist: Require excavation temporary works to be designed and independently checked by qualified engineers.
Require monitoring with instruments, trigger levels, defined actions and a named responsible person.
Write in that triggers cannot change without the design engineer's written agreement and notice to you.
Make monitoring a standing meeting item, reported even when there is no exception.
Require dewatering contingency: standby pumps, alarms and weekend-proof power.
Commission a dilapidation survey of neighbouring structures before breaking ground.
Treat cloudy water through a retaining wall as a stop-work condition.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A wall deflection reading exceeds its review trigger two weeks running, and the contractor writes proposing higher triggers because the wall is 'performing well'. How do you reply?
selftest.a: Decline until the design engineer has investigated why movement exceeds prediction, rechecked the design with the measured data, and agreed any change in writing with notice to you. Investigate, then revise; never revise, then continue. That is the Nicoll Highway lesson. Ask for increased monitoring frequency in the meantime.

apply: Write the two-sentence contract clause you would use to stop monitoring trigger levels being changed without the engineer's written agreement and notice to the owner.
sources: Nicoll Highway collapse (Singapore, 2004) summarised from public accounts of the Committee of Inquiry; read the primary report before quoting details [unverified — confirm independently]. Monitoring practice follows common geotechnical practice. Soil unit weights are typical values. Example hypothetical.

title: What the Code Fixes About Your Ground Before You Draw Anything
summary: The IBC is a model code with no force until a jurisdiction adopts it, so compliance is always local and edition-specific. Three of its chapters bear on the ground: soils and foundations, flood design, and special inspections the owner engages and pays for.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the building code decides several things about your ground before anyone draws a footing: how the soil must be investigated, where your plant may sit relative to flood level, and who checks the work on your behalf. Know the adopted edition first, because the model code alone binds nobody.

In plain English

The International Building Code is a model code published by the International Code Council. It has no legal force until a state, county or city adopts it, usually with local amendments, and adoption happens at a particular edition. So "the code" for your building means a specific edition as amended by your jurisdiction. Many places outside the United States use their own codes, and some reference American standards selectively. The first deliverable on any project is a written statement of which code and which amendments govern, from a local code professional.

Chapter 18: soils and foundations

The soils and foundations chapter requires a geotechnical investigation in many circumstances, sets requirements for foundations, and includes a table of presumptive load-bearing values that may be used for some soils without a site-specific investigation [unverified — confirm independently]. On a building of consequence, decline presumptive values. They are deliberately conservative, so you pay for larger foundations, and they still leave you carrying unmeasured ground risk, including settlement, which a bearing value says nothing about.

Flood design

Where the site is in a flood hazard area, the IBC structural chapter and the standard it references, ASCE 24, Flood Resistant Design and Construction, govern how high the lowest floor must be and what may be placed below the design flood elevation [unverified — confirm independently]. That second point is a one-way door on plant room location: switchgear, a standby generator, fire pumps and lift machinery generally belong above flood level or in a protected enclosure, and moving them after the design is fixed is expensive. Confirm early where flood rules permit them.

Chapter 17: special inspections

The special inspections chapter requires independent inspection of specified work, such as soils, concrete, steel connections and some fire-resistant construction, by qualified inspectors, documented in a Statement of Special Inspections prepared by the registered design professional [unverified — confirm independently]. The code generally requires the owner, or the owner's agent other than the contractor, to engage and pay the inspection agency. That is the code deliberately putting the quality check on the owner's side of the incentive line.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical interior column load of 1,500 kilonewtons on a pad footing.

  1. With a presumptive allowable bearing value of 75 kilopascals, the pad area is 1,500 divided by 75, which is 20 square metres, a pad about 4.5 metres square.
  2. With a site-specific investigation giving an allowable of 150 kilopascals, the area is 1,500 divided by 150, which is 10 square metres, a pad about 3.2 metres square.
  3. Half the footing area means roughly half the excavation, concrete and reinforcement for that element. Across forty columns the saving can exceed the cost of the investigation several times over.
  4. And the presumptive route still gave no settlement estimate. On soft clay, settlement usually governs, as Week Seven shows.

Now the flood check. If the design flood elevation is 12.00 metres plus freeboard and the basement plant room floor sits at 9.50, the switchgear location is already in conflict with flood rules, and the time to discover it is concept stage.

The certificate of occupancy

The certificate of occupancy is the document that lets people use the building. It depends on final inspections, special inspection reports and life safety systems being accepted. Track it as a project deliverable with its own critical path, because it is the document that turns a building into revenue.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is carrying a code assumption from another project or another jurisdiction. Editions differ, amendments differ, and a figure that held elsewhere may be wrong here.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner lets the special inspection engagement migrate to the contractor because it is administratively simpler. The inspector then reports to the party whose work he inspects. Engage the agency yourself, under your own contract, reporting to you.

How you will use it

Get a written statement of the governing code and amendments. Commission a code analysis at concept stage covering occupancy, construction type, height and area, flood requirements and foundation provisions. Instruct in writing that presumptive bearing values are not to replace a site-specific investigation. Ask for the Statement of Special Inspections early so its cost is known before award. Professional sign-off required: a local code consultant, the registered design professional, and the building official.
checklist: Get a written statement of the governing code edition and local amendments.
Commission a code analysis at concept stage, including flood and foundation provisions.
Instruct in writing that presumptive bearing values are not to replace a site investigation.
Confirm early where flood rules permit plant rooms, switchgear, generator and fire pump.
Ask for the Statement of Special Inspections early, so its cost is known before award.
Engage the special inspection agency yourself, reporting to you.
Track the certificate of occupancy as a deliverable with its own critical path.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: To save time, the design team proposes presumptive bearing values from the code table instead of waiting for the site investigation. What is wrong with that on a mid-rise building over clay?
selftest.a: Presumptive values are conservative, so the footings get bigger and dearer, and they say nothing about settlement, which usually governs on clay. You pay for caution and still carry the unmeasured risk. Wait for, or accelerate, the site-specific investigation and require a settlement estimate.

apply: Write the one-paragraph request you would send a local code consultant asking for the governing code edition, amendments, flood requirements and special inspection obligations for a hypothetical site.
sources: IBC (International Code Council) Chapters 16, 17, 18 and ASCE 24 as commonly cited; requirements, table values and chapter numbering vary by edition and local adoption [unverified — confirm independently]. Verify against the current adopted edition. Example hypothetical.

title: Who Pays When the Ground Is Not What You Were Told
summary: Pushing all ground risk onto the contractor does not remove it: the careful bidder prices it and the careless one leaves it out, wins, and claims later. The mature position is to investigate, disclose the facts, and fix a baseline so a surprise becomes a measurement.
body:
Mr Shabazz, ground risk transferred is ground risk priced, and usually priced badly. The owner who investigates properly, discloses everything and fixes a measurable baseline pays less than the owner who hides the report behind a disclaimer.

In plain English

Nobody knows exactly what is under a site until it is dug. When the ground differs from what was expected, someone pays for the extra digging, dewatering, rock breaking or redesign. The contract decides who. A differing site conditions clause is the standard American mechanism for answering that question in advance.

The two types

Standard American clauses, in federal contracts and in forms such as AIA A201, recognise two types of differing condition. The first is a condition that differs materially from what the contract documents indicated. The second is an unusual condition, of a kind that differs materially from what is ordinarily encountered in work of that character in the area. Exact wording differs between forms and editions [unverified — confirm independently]. Both depend on prompt written notice, usually before the condition is disturbed, so the owner can see it.

Why hiding the report backfires

An owner may be tempted to withhold the geotechnical report, or to attach a blanket disclaimer saying bidders may not rely on it. The paperwork looks tidier and the exposure grows. Careful bidders add a large premium for unknown ground. Careless bidders price nothing, win, and recover through claims, and courts in many jurisdictions treat broad disclaimers with suspicion where the owner held relevant information [unverified — confirm independently]. Either way the owner pays, once as premium or once as claim.

The baseline approach

The mature position is to investigate properly, disclose the facts, and fix a baseline. A geotechnical baseline report states contractual assumptions: for example, that rock will be encountered over no more than a stated volume, or that groundwater will be no higher than a stated level. Conditions within the baseline are the contractor's risk and priced in his bid. Conditions beyond it are the owner's, paid at agreed rates. A simpler version is a bidder's schedule of assumptions, where each bidder states what he assumed. Either way a surprise becomes a measurement, not a lawsuit.

A worked example

Suppose a hypothetical excavation where the baseline states that rock requiring breaking will not exceed 200 cubic metres, with an agreed rate of 100 per cubic metre for rock beyond baseline.

  1. The contractor prices 200 cubic metres of rock in his lump sum: 20,000 if his own rate matches.
  2. On site, the surveyed quantity of rock is 500 cubic metres. That is 300 cubic metres beyond baseline.
  3. Payment is 300 times 100, which is 30,000, plus any time on the critical path at the agreed weekly rate. Measured, priced and settled at the next valuation.
  4. Without a baseline, the contractor files a claim for an unquantified "materially different" condition, both sides hire experts, and the argument costs more than the rock.
  5. Had the owner hidden the report, a careful bidder might have added 60,000 for unknown rock and a careless bidder nothing, then claimed. Disclosure with a baseline costs 20,000 plus 30,000, with no dispute.

The negotiation thread

Leverage peaks before a preferred bidder is named, while competition still disciplines price. Concede what costs little and buys goodwill: fair unit rates for measured overruns and fair time for critical-path effects. Hold what protects you: the notice requirement (written notice before the condition is disturbed) and the measurement basis (surveyed quantities, not estimates). Inversion helps: ask how this clause would be used against you if the relationship soured.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a thin investigation paired with an aggressive disclaimer. It produces the highest bids from careful contractors, the lowest from careless ones, and the most disputes on site.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that writing "the contractor accepts all ground risk" makes the risk disappear. It changes who argues about it, and often turns a measurable quantity into litigation.

How you will use it

Fund a proper investigation, disclose it to bidders, and fix a baseline or require a schedule of assumptions. Agree unit rates for measured overruns and a weekly rate for time. Hold firm on written notice before disturbance and on surveyed measurement. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer to prepare the baseline; construction counsel for the clause.
checklist: Fund a proper investigation and disclose it to all bidders.
Fix a geotechnical baseline or require each bidder to state his assumptions.
Agree unit rates for measured quantities beyond the baseline.
Hold firm on written notice before a differing condition is disturbed.
Measure overruns by survey, not by estimate.
Avoid blanket no-reliance disclaimers on information you hold.
Use your leverage before naming a preferred bidder.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your counsel suggests attaching the geotechnical report to the tender with a clause saying bidders may not rely on it and accept all ground risk. Do you agree?
selftest.a: No. Careful bidders will price a large premium for unknown ground and careless ones will price nothing and claim later, and a broad disclaimer over information you hold may not hold up. Disclose the report, fix a baseline with agreed rates for measured overruns, and hold the notice and measurement provisions.

apply: Draft a two-line baseline statement for one hypothetical ground condition, such as rock volume or groundwater level, with the unit rate for quantities beyond it.
sources: Differing site conditions clauses as found in the US Federal Acquisition Regulation and AIA A201; wording and treatment of disclaimers vary by form, edition and jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently]. Geotechnical baseline reports follow published American tunnelling and underground practice. Example hypothetical.

title: Week Three Review: Investigation, Failure, Code and Contract
summary: Six scenario questions on reading a geotechnical investigation, recognising excavation failure patterns, the code's grip on the ground, and allocating ground risk by contract. The week's thread is that one investigation decision shows up as safety, code, cost and contract risk at once.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week treated the ground as four documents at once: a safety document, a code document, a cost document and a contract document. Answer each question before reading the answer.

Question 1. The seller hands you a geotechnical report: two boreholes to 5 metres, groundwater dipped once on the drilling day. Your engineer is considering a raft 22 metres wide. What is the report worth?

Answer. It is background, not a design document. A raft that wide stresses the ground to a depth far beyond 5 metres, a single water reading cannot support dewatering or uplift design, and two holes cannot describe variation across the footprint. Commission a supplementary investigation scoped to the raft, with deeper boreholes, cone profiles and groundwater monitored over time, addressed to you.

Question 2. A log shows CH at 4 metres with a high plasticity index, and peat at 7 metres. What do the two findings tell you?

Answer. CH is a high-plasticity clay, and a high plasticity index predicts movement through swelling and shrinkage, so it is a movement question as much as a strength one. Peat is organic and highly compressible, and keeps compressing for years. Peat under the footprint is a serious finding; the foundation must either bypass it or the design must account for long-term settlement.

Question 3. An inclinometer exceeds its review trigger for two weeks and the contractor proposes raising the triggers. What do you do?

Answer. Refuse until the design engineer has investigated the cause, rechecked the design with measured data and agreed any change in writing with notice to you. Increase monitoring in the meantime. Investigate, then revise; never revise, then continue. That is the Nicoll Highway lesson.

Question 4. To save time, the team suggests presumptive bearing values. What is the cost of saying yes?

Answer. Bigger footings, because presumptive values are conservative, and no settlement estimate, which on soft ground usually governs. For a 1,500 kilonewton column, a presumptive 75 kilopascals needs 20 square metres of footing against 10 at a measured 150. You pay for caution and still carry unmeasured risk.

Question 5. Who should engage and pay the special inspection agency, and why does it matter?

Answer. The owner, or the owner's agent other than the contractor, as the IBC special inspection provisions generally require (verify against the adopted edition). It matters because the person who pays the inspector shapes how judgement calls go. An inspector paid by the contractor reports to the party whose work he checks.

Question 6. The baseline allows 150 cubic metres of rock at the contractor's risk, with 120 per cubic metre beyond. The survey measures 400 cubic metres. What is owed?

Answer. 400 minus 150 is 250 cubic metres beyond baseline, times 120, which is 30,000, plus any critical-path time at the agreed weekly rate, subject to the contractor having given written notice before the rock was disturbed. Without a baseline, the same rock becomes an argument about what "materially different" means.

Recap

Soil is grains, water and air. Coarse soils carry load by friction and fail suddenly; fine soils carry it by cohesion and fail slowly, through settlement. The plasticity index predicts movement, and organics under the footprint are a serious finding. SPT gives samples; CPT gives a continuous profile; good practice on variable ground uses both, with groundwater monitored over time.

Investigation depth is set by the foundation actually proposed, and an inherited report is background only. Read the logs yourself and mark every hedge.

Ground works fail four ways: collapsing faces, failing support systems, groundwater from below, and damage to neighbours. Monitoring works only if triggers are fixed and changed only by the engineer in writing, and cloudy water through a wall means stop.

The code binds only as adopted, at an edition, with local amendments. Decline presumptive bearing values on a building of consequence, settle plant locations against flood rules at concept stage, and engage the special inspector yourself.

Ground risk transferred is ground risk priced. Investigate, disclose, and fix a baseline so a surprise becomes a measurement. Hold the notice and measurement terms.

The thread: one cheap economy on site investigation injures safety, code compliance, cost and contract risk at the same time, and when several disciplines point at the same action from different directions, that is usually the action. Professional sign-off required: geotechnical engineer, a local code consultant, the building official, and construction counsel.

Next week opens the hole itself: the rules for keeping people safe in it, the shape that decides its volume, the water that has to come out of it, and the lender who is watching the first money disappear into it.
checklist: Scope the investigation to the foundation actually proposed.
Read the plasticity index and organics in every log.
Hold trigger levels fixed unless the engineer changes them in writing.
Decline presumptive bearing values on a building of consequence.
Engage and pay the special inspector yourself.
Fix a ground baseline with agreed rates for measured overruns.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Name one decision this week that affects safety, code compliance, cost and contract risk at the same time.
selftest.a: Funding a properly scoped site investigation. It informs excavation safety and monitoring, satisfies the code's foundation requirements without presumptive values, reduces footing cost and contingency, and makes a ground baseline possible so differing conditions are measured rather than litigated.

apply: Write, from memory, the five things to look for in a borehole log and the two types of differing site condition, then check them.
sources: Review of Lessons 11 to 14; see those lessons for sources. Code provisions to be verified against the current adopted edition. Figures hypothetical.
